prompt: What does version control give a project that keeping dated copies of the folder does not?
optionA: A safe copy of the current files
optionB: A recorded history that can be returned to, with a note of what each change was
optionC: A way of sending files to other people
optionD: Somewhere to keep files that are too large for a disk
correctAnswerText: A recorded history that can be returned to, with a note of what each change was
explanation: Dated copies preserve states without saying anything about them, whereas version control keeps a recorded history that can be returned to, with a note of what each change was. Being able to ask which change did what is the part copying cannot provide.

prompt: Does a project under version control save the work automatically as it is typed?
optionA: Yes; every change is captured as it is made
optionB: Yes; a snapshot is taken every few minutes
optionC: Yes; each time the editor saves the file
optionD: No; work enters the history only when it is deliberately recorded
correctAnswerText: No; work enters the history only when it is deliberately recorded
explanation: Recording is an act somebody performs, so work enters the history only when it is deliberately recorded. Believing otherwise is exactly why unrecorded work gets lost.

prompt: A file is deleted by accident, a week after the change to it was recorded. What can version control do?
optionA: Bring the file back as it was in the recorded history
optionB: Nothing; it records changes rather than files
optionC: Bring it back only if the folder was copied beforehand
optionD: Bring back only the most recent version of the whole project
correctAnswerText: Bring the file back as it was in the recorded history
explanation: Anything that was recorded remains available, so version control can bring the file back as it was in the recorded history. No separate copy of the folder is needed for that.

prompt: Why does each recorded change carry a written message?
optionA: So the changed file can be found again by name
optionB: Because the tool refuses to store anything without text
optionC: So the history says why a change was made, and not only what altered
optionD: To record who was sitting at the machine
correctAnswerText: So the history says why a change was made, and not only what altered
explanation: The message is the part a person reads months later, so the history says why a change was made, and not only what altered. The difference between the two states is already recorded without it.

prompt: A student copies their project folder every evening and keeps the copies. What does that practice still not give them?
optionA: A second copy of the files
optionB: The ability to see which individual change caused something and to return to just that point
optionC: Protection against the disk failing
optionD: The ability to work without a network
correctAnswerText: The ability to see which individual change caused something and to return to just that point
explanation: Nightly copies give states of a whole day and nothing finer, so they lack the ability to see which individual change caused something and to return to just that point. A day's work arrives as one undivided lump.

prompt: Besides the files as they stand now, what does a repository hold?
optionA: Only the files as they stand now
optionB: A link to the website the project came from
optionC: The settings of the editor being used
optionD: The recorded history of the project
correctAnswerText: The recorded history of the project
explanation: A repository is the project plus the recorded history of the project, which is what makes earlier states reachable. Without the history it would be an ordinary folder.

prompt: Does starting a repository require an account on a website?
optionA: No; it exists on the machine where it was created
optionB: Yes; a repository lives on a website by definition
optionC: Yes, unless the project is never shared with anybody
optionD: Only once the first change has been recorded
correctAnswerText: No; it exists on the machine where it was created
explanation: Creating a repository is a local act, so it exists on the machine where it was created. Sharing it later is a separate decision that adds a second copy.

prompt: For a repository on your own machine, where is the recorded history kept?
optionA: On the website the project is shared through
optionB: In the editor that opened the project
optionC: Inside the project folder itself
optionD: In a backup folder elsewhere on the disk
correctAnswerText: Inside the project folder itself
explanation: The history travels with the project, because it is kept inside the project folder itself. Copying the folder copies the history along with it.

prompt: A project has been under version control on one laptop for six months and has never been shared with anybody. Is its history real?
optionA: No; a history only begins once the project is shared
optionB: Yes; a complete history exists locally with no shared copy involved
optionC: Only the most recent recorded change is kept
optionD: Yes, but it is discarded when the machine is restarted
correctAnswerText: Yes; a complete history exists locally with no shared copy involved
explanation: Nothing about a history depends on anybody else seeing it, so yes; a complete history exists locally with no shared copy involved. What such a project lacks is a second copy, not a history.

prompt: What does git add do?
optionA: Records the change into the history
optionB: Sends the change to the shared copy
optionC: Creates a new file in the project
optionD: Marks a change to be included in the next recorded commit
correctAnswerText: Marks a change to be included in the next recorded commit
explanation: It moves a change one step along, no further: it marks a change to be included in the next recorded commit. Nothing is written into the history until a commit is made.

prompt: What does git commit do?
optionA: Records the marked changes into the local history
optionB: Marks changes so that they can be recorded later
optionC: Sends the recorded changes to the shared copy
optionD: Brings other people's changes down from the shared copy
correctAnswerText: Records the marked changes into the local history
explanation: A commit records the marked changes into the local history and stops there. Reaching the shared copy takes a further command.

prompt: What does git log do?
optionA: Records a new change into the history
optionB: Sends the history to the shared copy
optionC: Shows the recorded history without changing anything
optionD: Removes the oldest entries from the history
correctAnswerText: Shows the recorded history without changing anything
explanation: It is a reading command, so it shows the recorded history without changing anything. Nothing it prints alters the project or the history.

prompt: A change has just been committed. Is it now on the shared copy?
optionA: Yes; committing publishes the change
optionB: No; committing records it locally, and sending it is a separate step
optionC: Yes, once the editor is closed
optionD: Only if the file was marked before being committed
correctAnswerText: No; committing records it locally, and sending it is a separate step
explanation: The two acts are deliberately separate, so no; committing records it locally, and sending it is a separate step. Believing the commit published it is what leaves a teammate looking at old code.

prompt: A file has been edited and marked for the next commit, and no commit has been made. Is the change in the history?
optionA: Yes; marking it records it
optionB: Partly; the first half of the change is recorded
optionC: Yes, as soon as the editor saves the file
optionD: No; marking it only says it should go into the next commit
correctAnswerText: No; marking it only says it should go into the next commit
explanation: Marking and recording are different steps, so no; marking it only says it should go into the next commit. Until the commit runs, the history is unchanged.

prompt: A file is edited, marked for the next commit, edited a second time, and then committed with no further marking. Which version was recorded?
optionA: The version as it stood when it was marked
optionB: The version as it stood at the moment of the commit
optionC: Both versions, as two entries
optionD: Nothing, because the file changed after being marked
correctAnswerText: The version as it stood when it was marked
explanation: Marking captures the content at that moment, so the version as it stood when it was marked is what the commit recorded. The second edit is still sitting in the folder, unrecorded.

prompt: Three files have been changed and only one of them has been marked. A commit is made. Which changes does it record?
optionA: The changes to all three files
optionB: The change to whichever file was edited most recently
optionC: The change to the marked file only
optionD: None, because all three have to be marked first
correctAnswerText: The change to the marked file only
explanation: A commit records what was marked and nothing else, so it holds the change to the marked file only. The other two changes remain in the folder, unrecorded.

prompt: Two files were marked. One of the two was then edited again before the commit was made. How much does the commit hold, and in what form?
optionA: Both files, each as it stands now
optionB: Both files, with the re-edited one as it stood when it was marked
optionC: Only the file that was not edited again
optionD: Only the file that was edited again
correctAnswerText: Both files, with the re-edited one as it stood when it was marked
explanation: Marking fixes what will be recorded for each file separately, so the commit holds both files, with the re-edited one as it stood when it was marked. The later edit needs marking of its own before it can be recorded.

prompt: A brand new file notes.md is created in the project folder and nothing else is done. What does a status check report about it?
optionA: That it is marked to go into the next commit
optionB: That it has been recorded into the history
optionC: Nothing, because new files are picked up automatically
optionD: That it is a new file the project is not yet tracking
correctAnswerText: That it is a new file the project is not yet tracking
explanation: Creating a file is not a step in the recording sequence, so the status reports that it is a new file the project is not yet tracking. It has to be marked before it can be recorded.

prompt: The commands run were: edit a.txt, git add a.txt, git commit, then edit a.txt again. What state is a.txt in?
optionA: Recorded once, and changed again since that recording
optionB: Recorded, with nothing outstanding
optionC: Marked to go into the next commit
optionD: Not part of the project any more
correctAnswerText: Recorded once, and changed again since that recording
explanation: The commit captured the first edit and the second came afterwards, so a.txt is recorded once, and changed again since that recording. The second edit is unmarked and unrecorded.

prompt: Both a.txt and b.txt were edited, then only a.txt was marked before the commit ran. What is true of b.txt afterwards?
optionA: It was recorded alongside a.txt
optionB: It was removed from the folder by the commit
optionC: It is still in the folder with its change intact, and it is not in the history
optionD: Its change was discarded when the commit ran
correctAnswerText: It is still in the folder with its change intact, and it is not in the history
explanation: Committing takes what was marked and leaves everything else exactly as it was, so b.txt is still in the folder with its change intact, and it is not in the history. A commit never removes or discards unmarked work.

prompt: You have just committed a change. Can a teammate see it yet?
optionA: Yes; as soon as it is committed
optionB: No; not until it has been sent to the shared copy
optionC: Yes, once they reload the page they are looking at
optionD: Only if they happen to be online at that moment
correctAnswerText: No; not until it has been sent to the shared copy
explanation: The commit reached your own history and nothing else, so no; not until it has been sent to the shared copy. Their view of the project is built from what the shared copy holds.

prompt: You have made three commits today and sent none of them. What does the shared copy hold?
optionA: All three commits
optionB: The newest of the three commits
optionC: Nothing, since it is now out of step
optionD: The history as it stood before today's three commits
correctAnswerText: The history as it stood before today's three commits
explanation: Nothing has travelled, so the shared copy holds the history as it stood before today's three commits. It is not out of step in the sense of being broken; it is simply older.

prompt: A student reports that a month of work has disappeared after their laptop was wiped and rebuilt. They had committed everything carefully and had never sent anything. Where does the work exist now?
optionA: Nowhere; the only copy was the local history on that laptop
optionB: On the shared copy, since everything was committed
optionC: On the shared copy, but only the most recent commit
optionD: Still on the laptop, recoverable through the editor
correctAnswerText: Nowhere; the only copy was the local history on that laptop
explanation: Committing carefully protected the work from mistakes inside the folder and from nothing else, so it exists nowhere; the only copy was the local history on that laptop. Sending is what puts a copy somewhere the machine cannot take with it.

prompt: You send your commits to the shared copy. Do your teammate's commits arrive on your machine at the same time?
optionA: Yes; sending exchanges work in both directions
optionB: Yes, as long as nothing conflicts
optionC: No; bringing changes down is a separate step
optionD: Only their most recent commit arrives
correctAnswerText: No; bringing changes down is a separate step
explanation: Sending moves work one way only, so no; bringing changes down is a separate step. Nothing arrives until it is asked for.

prompt: You have two commits and also some edits you have not committed. You send. What reaches the shared copy?
optionA: Everything currently in the folder
optionB: The two commits only; the uncommitted edits stay on your machine
optionC: Nothing, until the edits are committed as well
optionD: The uncommitted edits, which are the newest work
correctAnswerText: The two commits only; the uncommitted edits stay on your machine
explanation: Only recorded work can travel, so the two commits only reach the shared copy; the uncommitted edits stay on your machine. They are not refused; they were never part of what was sent.

prompt: You bring your teammate's changes down while holding your own uncommitted edits to a different file that nobody else touched. What happens to your edits?
optionA: They are overwritten by the incoming version of the project
optionB: They are committed automatically as part of the operation
optionC: They are discarded so that the incoming work can be applied
optionD: They are left exactly as they are
correctAnswerText: They are left exactly as they are
explanation: Incoming work only touches what it actually changes, and nobody else changed that file, so your edits are left exactly as they are. Uncommitted edits to a file the incoming work does change are the case that is refused instead.

prompt: A history is listed newest first: Fix totals rounding; Add export button; Add report page; Start the project. Which change was made first?
optionA: Start the project
optionB: Fix totals rounding
optionC: Add export button
optionD: Add report page
correctAnswerText: Start the project
explanation: The listing runs newest first, so the earliest change is the one at the bottom, Start the project. Reading the list top-down as a sequence of events reverses the chronology.

prompt: From that same listing, which entry introduced the export button?
optionA: Fix totals rounding, since it is the newest entry
optionB: Start the project, since the project contains it now
optionC: Add export button
optionD: Add report page, since the button is on that page
correctAnswerText: Add export button
explanation: Each entry records the change its message describes, so the button arrived with Add export button. The newest entry describes only the change it made.

prompt: A newcomer reads only the newest message in that listing and concludes that the project is a rounding fix. What have they misread?
optionA: The listing is ordered oldest first, so they read the wrong end
optionB: A message describes one change, while the project is the result of all the changes together
optionC: The newest entry replaces the ones before it
optionD: The messages describe intentions rather than changes that were made
correctAnswerText: A message describes one change, while the project is the result of all the changes together
explanation: The order was read correctly and the meaning was not: a message describes one change, while the project is the result of all the changes together. Reading the whole list is what describes the project.

prompt: A file is added to the ignore list before it has ever been recorded. What happens to that file?
optionA: It is deleted from the folder
optionB: It is hidden so the editor cannot open it
optionC: It is recorded once and then left alone
optionD: It stays in the folder and is never offered for recording
correctAnswerText: It stays in the folder and is never offered for recording
explanation: Ignoring changes what the tool pays attention to and not what exists, so the file stays in the folder and is never offered for recording. It is fully usable by everything else on the machine.

prompt: An ignored file is edited heavily. What does a status check report about it?
optionA: Nothing at all
optionB: That it has changed, marked as ignored
optionC: That it is waiting to be recorded
optionD: A warning that an ignored file was modified
correctAnswerText: Nothing at all
explanation: An ignored file is outside what the tool reports on, so a status check says nothing at all about it. Silence here is the expected result rather than a sign of a problem.

prompt: A configuration file was committed months ago. It has now been added to the ignore list, and it still keeps appearing as changed. Why?
optionA: The entry in the ignore list is spelled wrongly
optionB: The ignore list takes effect only after the next commit
optionC: Ignoring applies to files that are not already recorded, and this one is
optionD: The file has to be edited once more before ignoring starts
correctAnswerText: Ignoring applies to files that are not already recorded, and this one is
explanation: The file is already part of the recorded project, and ignoring applies to files that are not already recorded, and this one is. It has to be removed from tracking before the ignore entry has any effect.

prompt: A project folder is deleted. It held commits that had been sent, commits that had not been sent, and edits that were never committed. What survives?
optionA: Everything, because the project was under version control
optionB: Only the commits that had been sent
optionC: Every commit, whether it had been sent or not
optionD: Nothing whatever
correctAnswerText: Only the commits that had been sent
explanation: Only a copy that lives somewhere else survives the folder, so only the commits that had been sent do. Being under version control protects nothing that never left the folder.

prompt: Work that had been marked for the next commit, but not committed, was lost with the folder. A student says marking it should have protected it. Why did it not?
optionA: Marking protects text files but not other kinds
optionB: The marking is cleared whenever the machine shuts down
optionC: The deletion removed the marking before it could take effect
optionD: Marking only says what the next commit will contain, and stores nothing outside that folder
correctAnswerText: Marking only says what the next commit will contain, and stores nothing outside that folder
explanation: Marking is a step towards recording rather than a place of safety: it only says what the next commit will contain, and stores nothing outside that folder. It is one step short of even a local copy.

prompt: The goal is to get the change currently in the folder into the local history, and to do nothing else. What achieves exactly that?
optionA: Mark the change, then commit it
optionB: Mark the change
optionC: Mark the change, commit it, then send it
optionD: Send the project to the shared copy
correctAnswerText: Mark the change, then commit it
explanation: Two steps are needed and only two, so the answer is to mark the change, then commit it. Sending as well would achieve the goal and more than the goal.

prompt: Everything wanted is already committed locally. The goal is to let a teammate see that work, changing nothing else about the project. What achieves exactly that?
optionA: Commit again with a clearer message
optionB: Bring their changes down first, which carries yours up as part of the exchange
optionC: Send the commits to the shared copy
optionD: Mark every file again and commit
correctAnswerText: Send the commits to the shared copy
explanation: The work is recorded and simply has not travelled, so send the commits to the shared copy. Bringing their changes down moves work in the other direction only and would also alter the local project.

prompt: A teammate cannot see your change. Your own history shows the commit, and the shared copy does not. Which step was missed?
optionA: The change was never marked
optionB: The commit was never sent
optionC: The change was never committed
optionD: The teammate has not looked recently enough
correctAnswerText: The commit was never sent
explanation: The change reached your history and stopped there, so the commit was never sent. Both earlier steps clearly happened, because the commit exists.

prompt: Your history does not contain the change at all. The file in the folder contains it, and a status check lists the file as changed. Which step was missed?
optionA: The change was committed but never sent
optionB: The file is on the ignore list
optionC: The history listing is being filtered
optionD: The change was never committed
correctAnswerText: The change was never committed
explanation: The status check proves the tool can see the file and the history proves nothing was recorded, so the change was never committed. An ignored file would not be listed as changed at all.

prompt: Three omissions produce the same complaint that a change is missing: it was never marked, never committed, or never sent. Which single check separates them fastest?
optionA: Look at the local history: if the commit is absent it was never committed, and if it is present it was never sent
optionB: Send again and see whether the teammate can see it
optionC: Ask the teammate to look again in a few minutes
optionD: Redo the whole sequence from the beginning
correctAnswerText: Look at the local history: if the commit is absent it was never committed, and if it is present it was never sent
explanation: The local history divides the three cases in one look: if the commit is absent it was never committed, and if it is present it was never sent. Marking is then separated from committing by the status check, which is the second question rather than the first.

prompt: Somebody repeats the whole sequence — mark, commit, send — and the missing change appears. What has that established about the original cause?
optionA: That the change had never been marked
optionB: That the send had failed the first time
optionC: Nothing; every step was repeated, so it cannot say which one had been missed
optionD: That the shared copy had been out of date
correctAnswerText: Nothing; every step was repeated, so it cannot say which one had been missed
explanation: Repeating everything guarantees the outcome and destroys the evidence: nothing; every step was repeated, so it cannot say which one had been missed. The same person will meet the same problem next week with nothing learned.

prompt: The change is in your history and on the shared copy, and the teammate still cannot see it in their project. What is left to explain it?
optionA: The change was never committed after all
optionB: They have not brought the newer commits down into their own copy
optionC: The file is on the ignore list
optionD: The send reported success but did nothing
correctAnswerText: They have not brought the newer commits down into their own copy
explanation: Both copies you can inspect contain the change, so the remaining gap is on their side: they have not brought the newer commits down into their own copy. Their folder is as old as their last fetch.

prompt: A file was deleted and that deletion was committed. Three further commits have been made since, and all three are wanted. What restores the file without losing them?
optionA: Undo the last four commits
optionB: Delete the folder and fetch a fresh copy from the shared copy
optionC: Nothing; the file is gone from the project
optionD: Take the file back from the commit before the deletion and record that as a new change
correctAnswerText: Take the file back from the commit before the deletion and record that as a new change
explanation: The wanted work sits after the mistake, so the repair has to move forwards rather than backwards: take the file back from the commit before the deletion and record that as a new change. Undoing four commits would take the three wanted ones with it.

prompt: An hour of work that was never committed has been lost. Can the history bring it back?
optionA: No; the history holds only what was recorded into it
optionB: Yes, from the shared copy
optionC: Yes, from the marked-but-uncommitted work
optionD: Yes, from the most recent commit
correctAnswerText: No; the history holds only what was recorded into it
explanation: Recovery reaches exactly as far back as recording did, so no; the history holds only what was recorded into it. The most recent commit restores the state before the hour began, which is not the same as recovering the hour.

prompt: A bad commit can be undone by rewriting the history so that it never existed, or by recording a new commit that reverses its effect. What does the rewrite cost once the bad commit has already been shared?
optionA: Nothing; the rewritten history is simply tidier
optionB: The reversing approach becomes impossible afterwards
optionC: Everybody else still holds it, and their history no longer agrees with yours
optionD: The files themselves are lost along with the entry
correctAnswerText: Everybody else still holds it, and their history no longer agrees with yours
explanation: A rewrite changes only your copy, so everybody else still holds it, and their history no longer agrees with yours. A reversing commit costs a visible entry and keeps every copy in step.

prompt: A student fixes a confusing project state by deleting the folder and fetching a fresh copy from the shared copy. What have they lost?
optionA: Nothing; the shared copy holds the whole project
optionB: Every commit that had not been sent, and every edit that had not been committed
optionC: Only the edits that had not been committed
optionD: Only the most recent commit
correctAnswerText: Every commit that had not been sent, and every edit that had not been committed
explanation: The fresh copy contains what was sent and nothing else, so they have lost every commit that had not been sent, and every edit that had not been committed. It is the most common way of destroying real work while apparently doing something safe.

prompt: Three pieces of work exist: one committed and sent, one committed but not sent, and one edited but never committed. Which of them can be recovered from the shared copy alone?
optionA: All three of them
optionB: The two that were committed
optionC: None of them
optionD: Only the one that was committed and sent
correctAnswerText: Only the one that was committed and sent
explanation: The shared copy holds exactly what reached it, so only the one that was committed and sent can come back from there. The other two exist on the local machine or nowhere.

prompt: You and a teammate have both changed the project since the last time it was shared. Which order of operations loses nothing?
optionA: Commit your work, bring theirs down, settle anything that clashes, then send
optionB: Send first, so that your work is in place before theirs
optionC: Bring theirs down first, before committing your own work
optionD: Copy your files aside, bring theirs down, then copy yours back over
correctAnswerText: Commit your work, bring theirs down, settle anything that clashes, then send
explanation: Recording your work first makes it recoverable whatever happens next, so commit your work, bring theirs down, settle anything that clashes, then send. Every other order either risks your work or quietly discards theirs.

prompt: Why is committing before bringing other people's work down the safer order?
optionA: It makes the incoming work arrive faster
optionB: It prevents clashes from happening at all
optionC: Your work is recorded before anything else touches the folder, so it can be recovered whatever follows
optionD: It sends your work up at the same time
correctAnswerText: Your work is recorded before anything else touches the folder, so it can be recovered whatever follows
explanation: The risky moment is when somebody else's changes land in your folder, and committing first means your work is recorded before anything else touches the folder, so it can be recovered whatever follows. Clashes still happen; they simply stop being dangerous.

prompt: Copying your files aside, bringing the shared work down, and copying your files back over does keep your own work. What does it cost?
optionA: Nothing; it is the simplest approach available
optionB: It silently overwrites whatever your teammate changed in those same files
optionC: It loses your own work instead of theirs
optionD: It leaves the history unreadable afterwards
correctAnswerText: It silently overwrites whatever your teammate changed in those same files
explanation: The copy back is a blind overwrite, so it silently overwrites whatever your teammate changed in those same files. Nothing reports the loss, because as far as the tool is concerned you simply made those changes yourself.

prompt: An attempt to send is refused, with a message saying the shared copy holds work you do not have. What does that refusal protect against?
optionA: Sending a file that is too large to store
optionB: Recording a commit without a message
optionC: Two people editing the same line of the same file
optionD: Replacing your teammate's commits with a history that never contained them
correctAnswerText: Replacing your teammate's commits with a history that never contained them
explanation: Your history does not include their commits, so sending it as it stands would mean replacing your teammate's commits with a history that never contained them. The refusal is what forces you to bring their work down first.
